Chapter 6: The Machinery of Control—How Bureaucracy Sustains Itself
Isn’t it strange, how something that starts out promising freedom can, over time, twist itself into a tool for control? By the late 1930s, Soviet bureaucracy had crept into every part of daily life—not just through official rules or government orders, but through the little habits, the quiet expectations, and those subtle threats you could feel but rarely see.
The people running the system… they’d figured out how to keep the gears turning. Sometimes, sure, with brute force—but more often, it was those countless little pressures. The kind that shape what people do, what they say, even what they let themselves think.
Imagine a mid-level manager in a state-run factory. Not some movie villain, just an ordinary guy, trying to hang on to his job—and if he’s lucky, maybe get ahead a little. Every month, the bosses hand him targets that nobody could possibly reach. If he misses them, he could lose his job, or worse. But if he fudges the numbers? Well, that’s what everyone else is doing. Inspectors will turn a blind eye, as long as the paperwork looks right. So the real work—keeping the machines running, making sure workers show up, actually hitting production quotas—gets lost in a fog of endless reports and signatures.
That’s the secret of how bureaucracy protects itself. It rewards loyalty, not honesty. It cares more about how things look than how they really are. Most people figure out pretty quickly that playing along is safer than speaking up. A teacher who tries something new in her classroom? She drowns in paperwork. A doctor who questions hospital rules? Quietly reassigned. The message couldn’t be clearer: don’t rock the boat, and you’ll be left alone.
And it’s not just about following rules—it’s about knowing the right people. Who you know matters way more than what you know. A talented young engineer without connections? His ideas gather dust. Meanwhile, someone less skilled but with the right friends climbs the ladder. Over time, people’s ambitions start to change. Instead of dreaming about changing the world, they just hope for a better apartment, a chance to take a vacation, maybe a little security for their family.
What really made the bureaucracy strong was its talent for making itself seem permanent—like no other way was possible. Most people didn’t even notice how their options kept shrinking, how hope slowly faded into resignation. They just did what they needed to get by. The machinery of control was all around them, but it had become almost invisible—woven into their daily routines and every small calculation of risk and reward.
But underneath all that, frustration simmered. People whispered complaints at home, swapped jokes about the absurdity of official life, and sometimes, when they felt especially brave, pushed back—just a little. The machinery of control was powerful, yes, but it wasn’t unbreakable. It relied on millions of people going along with it. And that obedience… was never truly complete.
